# Multi-Country ASEAN Manufacturing Footprint Strategy

## Core Strategic Principle

Footprint relocation fails when it's treated as a **country-selection exercise** driven by tariff headlines and wage tables. It succeeds when treated as a **product-flow architecture problem**: decompose the portfolio into transferable product families, match each to the country whose supplier ecosystem and rules-of-origin economics genuinely fit, sequence moves within the organization's actual engineering bandwidth, and preserve optionality as tariffs keep shifting. The goal is not the cheapest labor or the biggest incentive package — it's **the lowest risk-adjusted total landed cost with genuine, defensible origin compliance**.

---

## 1. Segment the Portfolio by Transfer Archetype, Not by Country

The first mistake is asking "Vietnam or Thailand?" before asking "which products can move, in what order?" Classify every product family on three axes: tariff exposure, engineering coupling, and origin feasibility.

| Archetype | Profile | Origin Feasibility | Destination Logic |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A: Mature, tariff-exposed volume lines** | Frozen designs, low engineering-change (ECO) frequency, high US/EU exposure, stable demand | BOM can realistically reach regional value content thresholds | **Move first** — this is the anchor plant's founding volume |
| **B: Labor-intensive subassemblies** | Weldments, harnesses, enclosures, kits, paint/finishing | High — transformation is inherently local | Satellite plant or qualified local partners; movable later |
| **C: Precision/complex lines** | Hydraulics, drivetrains, high-spec machining, calibration-heavy | Depends entirely on local supplier depth | Only to Thailand/Malaysia-tier ecosystems, or retain at home hub |
| **D: NPI and high-mix ETO** | Frequent ECOs, tight engineering iteration loops, low volume | Poor — change control would break origin documentation | **Keep at home hub**; redesign for transferability later |

**Selection rule for wave 1:** a product family qualifies only if it passes all four tests — (a) tariff delta × volume justifies transfer cost, (b) ECO frequency below a defined threshold, (c) BOM can plausibly reach **≥50–60% regional value content** (buffer above the ~40% ATIGA/RCEP norms), and (d) no single-source exotic components. This filter typically yields 2–4 candidate families, not 20.

---

## 2. Match Countries to Roles — Don't Crown a Winner

No ASEAN country wins on all five dimensions. The correct output is a **role assignment**, not a ranking.

| Country | Supplier Depth | Labor | Logistics | Incentives & Stability | Best-Fit Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Vietnam** | Fast-growing machining/electronics clusters (Hai Phong, Bac Ninh, Binh Duong); thinner in precision castings/tooling | Young, trainable, disciplined; wages rising 6–8%/yr; land scarce in hot zones | Deep-sea ports (Lach Huyen, Cai Mep); direct transpacific sailings | CIT holidays + zones (blunted by global minimum tax); stable, but **highest US transshipment scrutiny** | **Anchor** for assembly-led export volume |
| **Thailand** | Deepest mechanical base in ASEAN: automotive-grade castings, machining, tool & die, heat treat | Experienced engineers; aging workforce; higher wages | Laem Chabang + EEC corridor; reliable power | BOI holidays; periodic political churn but strong business continuity | **Precision/Archetype C hub**; regional machining center |
| **Indonesia** | Steel, castings, growing machining (Karawang–Cikarang belt); depth uneven | Scale and cost; skill gaps outside Java | Archipelago complexity; Tanjung Priok congestion; improving (Patimban) | Large
